description:
Flowering Interior Live Oak. Link to one with Acorns: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/250320996

Interior Live Oak (Quercus wislizeni), a.k.a Chapparal Oak, is a native Oak in the High-latitude Oaks (Quercus) Subgenus and in the Red Oaks (Lobatae) Section. It is found in Foothill Woodland and Chaparral plant communities. Leaves are mostly pliant and flat (not stiff and concave like Coast Live Oak, Quercus agrifolia), evergreen with smooth or spiny margins, dark green above and lighter below, and 1-4 inches long. Mature acorn is slender, about 1.25 inches long, cup covers almost half the nut, and acorn matures in second year. Acorn diagram: http://floranorthamerica.org/File:FNA03_P83_Quercus_pg_453.jpeg.

Indigenous people had many uses for this plant, medicinally and as food. 23 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Quercus+wislizeni

Per Jepson eFlora: "Habit: Shrub 2--4(6) m or tree generally 10--22 m, evergreen; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2--5 cm; petiole 3--15 mm; blade generally oblong to elliptic or lanceolate, adaxially glabrous, shiny, generally dark green, abaxially glabrous, +- shiny, yellow-green, tip generally acute, abruptly pointed, margin entire to spine-toothed, rarely wavy. Fruit: cup 12--18 mm wide, 12--16 mm deep, cup-shaped to hemispheric, scales not tubercled, +- thin; nut 20--40 mm, cylindric-ovoid, ovoid, or +- obconic, distally acute to +- obtuse, shell woolly inside; mature in year 2."
Jepson eFlora: https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=40780

This community occupies dry, rocky or gravelly slopes with either light or heavy soils at an elevation generally above that of coastal sage scrub, but adjacent to it. The boundary between chaparral and coastal sage scrub is not always a clear one, and many species may be found on either side of such a boundary."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

description:
Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia)

Plant Family: Fagaceae

Kumeyaay Name(s): sñaw (LH; SJ); siñao (SC); señao (Cortés Rodríguez); ‘esnyaaw (Hedges); isnyau (Spier)

Scientific Name: Quercus agrifolia

Common Name: Coast Live Oak

Location Information: Found in coastal regions of California, often in oak woodland and chaparral communities. 

Defining Features: Evergreen tree with thick, leathery leaves that are convex with spiny edges. The bark is dark gray and deeply furrowed. It produces small, elongated acorns (sñaw n'uur). It can grow up to 25 meters tall. 

Kumeyaay Uses: Acorns are a staple food source for the Kumeyaay. They are collected, cracked open, leeched for tannins, and processed into flour for various dishes. The wood was used for making tools, hunting weapons, and construction materials.

description:
Canyon Live Oak (Quercus chrysolepis), a.k.a. Canyon Oak, Golden Cup Oak or Maul Oak is a native, evergreen tree in the Beech (Fagaceae) family that grows in canyons and on slopes in many plant communities, including near the coast and in the desert. It is the most widely distributed Oak in California. Leaves are flat, not cupped, leathery, oblong to oblong- or round-ovate, adaxially (top-side) dark green, abaxially (underside) golden or pale, puberulent when young, and glabrous in age. Leaf tips are acute to abruptly pointed. Margins are variable and can be entire, or spine-toothed. Acorns are oblong, ovoid,  or elliptic. The cup is more distinctive. It is shallow with thick, sometimes tubercled scales and is covered with golden hairs when young. Peak bloom time: April-May. Peak flowering time: April-May.

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) A.k.a. CLO, is a native, long-lived tree (up to 125 - 250 years) in the High-latitude Oaks (Subgenus Quercus) and Beech (Fagaceae) family. Quercus agrifolia is by far the most common Oak tree on the Monterey Peninsula, CA. Leaves are evergreen, oval, cupped or spoon-shaped (adaxially convex). “Hairy armpits” at leaf veins on underside of CLO leaf distinguishes it from other Quercus species. Margins of mature leaves have sharp spines that are very noticeable when you sit in the leaf litter. Acorns (fruits) are long and slender.

Per Jepson eFlora: Coast Live Oak grows "(6)10--25 m, evergreen; top wide; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2.5--6(9) cm; petiole 4--15 mm; blade generally widely elliptic to round, generally adaxially convex, +- dull green, abaxially glabrous to densely tomentose, dull, pale green, tip rounded to spine-toothed, margin rolled under or not, weakly spine-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--16 mm wide, 8--15 mm deep, obconic, scales thin, +- not tubercled, +- glabrous, +- brown; nut 25--35 mm, slender, ovoid, distally acute, shell woolly inside; mature in year 1. "

What causes those fuzzy, white "hairy armpits" where primary vein meets 2ndary veins? Answer: Mite Apartments. Per INat fredwatson: "the prevailing hypothesis is that they function as dolmatia - places for arthopods to live - in this case, mites. There's an idea that the mites either eat fungi or prey on herbivores that would otherwise damage the leaf. A 2020 paper by Coltharp et al. found support for the dolmatium hypothesis, but didn't find support for the predation or fungivory - perhaps because of small sample size and not necessarily because the process doesn't occur. So, mites live there, and there might be a benefit to the tree."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

description:
Bull Creek butterfly count with Don Fraser; we were one of four groups and were the only group in Triple N Ranch WMA. The weather at the start was sunny and 78 degrees ("feels like" 85) with a light breeze. We drove two loops, for distances of about 17 miles driven and 3.5 miles walked over 7.5 hours. This was my first visit to Triple N, and it consists mostly of beautiful fire-maintained Longleaf Pine flatwoods. Possibly owing to the drought, few species were flowering (Nuttall's Thistles were nearly done for the year). We saw almost no Pickerelweed and no White Beggarticks. However, Rosy Camphorweed was abundant in places and in full bloom. Gray Hairstreaks were ridiculously abundant, mostly nectaring on Rosy Camphorweed; our group saw 168, and the total count for the four groups was 661! We did rather well with skipper diversity (our group got a few species missed otherwise), but numbers were very low. All records here represent different individuals. We met the other groups at the Triple N entrance at 1600 and left at 1649. The weather at the end was sunny and 95 degrees ("feels like" 104) with a light breeze. I got home at 2121.

Birds added to my Osceola County list were Red-bellied Woodpecker, Pileated Woodpecker, and Carolina Wren photographed or audio-recorded, and Brown-headed Nuthatch observed and photographed.

Don's and my butterfly totals were:

Zebra Swallowtail -- 7
Black Swallowtail -- 1
Giant Swallowtail -- 2
Spicebush Swallowtail -- 4
Palamedes Swallowtail -- 7

description: A solo visit to see what was around, and because I had not been out for eight days. Because of all the rain we have gotten the past few days -- and it is raining again as I write this -- I decided to avoid South Road and to stay on 3 Bridges Road and Gopher Road. As it turns out, I saw Julie Appleget on 3 Bridges Road and she said that she drove South Road earlier today. I did not stop along Rattlesnake Camp Road, so these records are solely from 3 Bridges Road (for its entire length) and Gopher Road. I saw very few nectar sources, so butterflies were pretty scarce; the only hotspot was a big clump of Tarflower, which attracted many swallowtails and one duskywing. I think I got two life moths if they get RGed. The weather at the start was sunny and 86 degrees ("feels like" 94) with a light breeze. I left at 1522, when the weather was sunny and 93 degrees ("feels like" 102) with a light breeze.

description:
There were a large number of Huckleberry Oaks in this region. This one had flowering catkins.

Huckleberry Oak (Quercus vacciniifolia) is mostly Endemic to  California. It is a native, prostrate to spreading, evergreen shrub in the Beech (Fagaceae) family that grows 3-5 ft tall on steep mountainous slopes, ridges, conifer and subalpine forests at elevation 150--2930 m. Leaves are alternate and simple with a single central vein. It has strong leaves to survive the snowy winters. Peak bloom time for the catkins: May-July. Indigenous people had many uses for Oaks (Quercus). 786 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Quercus+

Native American Ethnobotany: Traditional Native Plant Uses (medicines, foods, fibers, tools): http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Quercus+

Law's Field Guide to the Sierra Nevada, John Muir Laws, California Academy of Sciences, 2007, p. 50.

"Shrub < 1.5 m, prostrate to spreading, evergreen; twigs slender, pliable, glabrous. Leaf: 1.5--4 cm; petiole 3--6 mm; blade +- oblong, adaxially glabrous, green, abaxially glabrous, dull, pale green, tip obtuse to acute, margin entire to mucro-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--12 mm wide, 4--6 mm deep, thin, generally cup-shaped, scales +- tubercled to not; nut 10--15 mm, ovoid to +- spheric, distally obtuse to rounded; shell thin, subglabrous to sparsely tomentose inside; mature in year 2.
Ecology: Steep slopes, ridges, conifer forest, subalpine; Elevation: 150--2930 m."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general:

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

The abaxial appearance generally looks like QDG but with a lower density of hairs, and same with the texture of the adaxial surface, but the leaves were larger than usual and quite wide with unusually oblong margins. Based on the leaf shape and slightly scrubby growth habit, this probably has some scrub oak genes in it, but it was more arborescent and taller than the scrub oaks in the area.

Huckleberry Oak (Quercus vacciniifolia) is mostly Endemic to California. It is a native, prostrate to spreading, evergreen shrub in the Beech (Fagaceae) family that grows 3-5 ft tall on steep mountainous slopes, ridges, conifer and subalpine forests at elevation 150--2930 m. Leaves are alternate and simple with a single central vein. It has strong leaves to survive the snowy winters. Peak bloom time for the catkins: May-July. Indigenous people had many uses for Oaks (Quercus). 786 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Quercus+

"Shrub < 1.5 m, prostrate to spreading, evergreen; twigs slender, pliable, glabrous. Leaf: 1.5--4 cm; petiole 3--6 mm; blade +- oblong, adaxially glabrous, green, abaxially glabrous, dull, pale green, tip obtuse to acute, margin entire to mucro-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--12 mm wide, 4--6 mm deep, thin, generally cup-shaped, scales +- tubercled to not; nut 10--15 mm, ovoid to +- spheric, distally obtuse to rounded; shell thin, subglabrous to sparsely tomentose inside; mature in year 2.
Ecology: Steep slopes, ridges, conifer forest, subalpine; Elevation: 150--2930 m."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general:

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

I will post my camera photographs within the next week or so; I have 765 to sort through and mostly cull.

description:
Young Coast Live Oak with acorns. It should be a good winter for the Acorn Woodpeckers and other animals that depend on acorns. There seem to be many acorns forming on the CLO’s this year.
Flora of North America: Acorn diagram: http://floranorthamerica.org/File:FNA03_P83_Quercus_pg_453.jpeg 

My favorite Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) observations:
Fruiting (acorns): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/242561028
Mites--source of "hairy armpits" and Galls: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/219047085
Majestic Oak (with "hairy armpits" and acorns): https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/91810838
Flowering (catkins) and "hairy armpits": https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/141648110

COMPARE to similar-looking Interior Live Oak (Quercus wislizeni), a.k.a Chapparal Oak (that has less concave leaves), with Acorns: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/250320996

Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) A.k.a. CLO, is a native, long-lived tree (up to 125 - 250 years) in the High-latitude Oaks (Subgenus Quercus) and Beech (Fagaceae) family. Quercus agrifolia is by far the most common Oak tree on the Monterey Peninsula, CA. Leaves are evergreen, oval, cupped or spoon-shaped (adaxially convex). “Hairy armpits” at leaf veins on underside of CLO leaf distinguishes it from other Quercus species. Margins of mature leaves have sharp spines that are very noticeable when you sit in the leaf litter. Acorns (fruits) are long and slender.

Per Jepson eFlora: Coast Live Oak grows "(6)10--25 m, evergreen; top wide; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2.5--6(9) cm; petiole 4--15 mm; blade generally widely elliptic to round, generally adaxially convex, +- dull green, abaxially glabrous to densely tomentose, dull, pale green, tip rounded to spine-toothed, margin rolled under or not, weakly spine-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--16 mm wide, 8--15 mm deep, obconic, scales thin, +- not tubercled, +- glabrous, +- brown; nut 25--35 mm, slender, ovoid, distally acute, shell woolly inside; mature in year 1. "

Jepson eFlora https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=40530

Many organisms call CLO home. There is a whole INat project called "The wonderful diversity of life on Coast Live Oak" https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/the-wonderful-diversity-of-life-on-coast-live-oak. For example,

What causes those fuzzy, white "hairy armpits" where primary vein meets 2ndary veins? Answer: Mite Apartments. Per INat fredwatson: "the prevailing hypothesis is that they function as dolmatia - places for arthopods to live - in this case, mites. There's an idea that the mites either eat fungi or prey on herbivores that would otherwise damage the leaf. A 2020 paper by Coltharp et al. found support for the dolmatium hypothesis, but didn't find support for the predation or fungivory - perhaps because of small sample size and not necessarily because the process doesn't occur. So, mites live there, and there might be a benefit to the tree."

Flora of North America with botanical illustration: http://floranorthamerica.org/Quercus_agrifolia

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

This oak tree has been driving me acorns for years.  Sometimes I look at it, and it's a Coast Live; other times I go Ah ha it's an Interior Live.  There are a lot of for sure Coast Lives around, and some Interiors and Shreves per Calflora.  This one is pretty big, right next to the Miwok Shelter deck, leaves are all flat (not cupped), a bit longer than Coast Live, tend to have extra veins, arranged in a slightly more orderly fashion than Q. agrifolia.  Then I thought- maybe it's a hybrid!   It's certainly part Coast Live Oak.  I didn't make it up.  Plenty of those right next to it for comparison.  Throwing it out there.

description:
A solo visit 16-18 hours after the passage of Hurricane Milton, which made landfall as a Category 3 storm at Sarasota around 2100 last night. The weather at 1320 was sunny, 77 degrees ("feels like" 77), and breezy. I had intended to iNat the sandhills along both sides of 3 Bridges Road close to the northern end  of the WEA, but the usual wet spot along Thunder's Crossing Road was about 40 feet wide (although only maybe 6 inches deep, and with a rocky bottom) and I chose to not chance it in my Little Red. So I returned to Gopher Road and drove to its northern end. But I saw no nectar sources, so I turned back south to the spot north of the American Kestrel nestbox, where I found several Palatka Skippers in fall 2022. I had not been back since then because the area last burned in fall 2021 and I was not expecting any nectar sources. To my surprise, the area was ablaze with Coastal Plain Honeycombhead (Balduina angustifolia), which I love because it is the primary plant for Fuller's Flower Moths (Schinia fulleri), I spent two hours here, checking probably 800+ honeycombhead flowers.  I found one adult Fuller's, plus two caterpillars and one pupa presumed to be ths species. (I don't think any other butterfly or moth feeds on angustifolia).I stopped briefly at the little Redroot pond farther south, but it was a lake! I left the WEA at 1541 and headed home.

These are my cell-phone photographs, which are GPS-enabled.

description: A solo visit because I had not visited this site in 6 months! The weather at the start was clear, 77 degrees ("feels like" 77), and breezy. I walked all the usual trails in the usual order. I did not see a SINGLE Neotropical migrant! They all must have left last night. Almost all of the Coastal Plain Honeycombhead plants were knocked over by Hurricane Helene and/or Hurricane Milton, but I checked most (maybe 400) flowers for Schinia flower moths, finding none. Six trees (4 Sand Pines, 1 Turkey Oak, and 1 Red Maple) were toppled by Milton, but I got around or through all of them. The windy conditions ruled out macro photography with my cellphone. From 1030-1230, I conducted a stationary watch from the southern mound, the first time in several years that I have done this (there were no Mother Truckers in the Preserve today!). I left at 1234, when the weather was sunny, 79 ("feels like" 83), and breezy. It was an absolutely delightful day to be out!

description:
A solo visit because Deer Run Road, the road that leads to Perry Oldenburg Wildlife and Environmental Area nearby, was too flooded to risk Little Red. I decided to visit Chinsegut. The main entrance was gated off, with a sign that implied that there was no public access when the gate was closed. This was news to me, and apparently a new policy, as I have parked at the gate and walked in many times in the past. So, I drove back to very southern end of Chinsegut, parked there, and started walking. I walked counter-clockwise all the way around Mays Prairie and the entire WEA, back to the parking lot, a distance of 3.7 miles or more. There were numerous downed trees throughout the WEA (most of them oaks, but also some Longleaf Pines), and downed branches littered the ground. I left at 1413, when the weather was sunny, 84 degrees ("feels like" 87), with a light breeze.

description:
A solo visit -- Deer Run Road is no longer flooded over, so it was an easy drive in. The weather at the start was sunny and 77 degrees ("feels like" 77), with a light breeze/occasionally breezy. I walked the northern leg of the nature trail (flooded in places), then walked north along the powerlines, then northeast-curving-southeast to the eastern entrance, then west along the fenceline. After I crossed the powerlines, in an area that burned in spring 2024, I was astounded by the number of Coastal Plain Honeycombhead plants. I easily searched 2,000 individual flowers for Fuller's Flower Moths, finding ZERO! But, I found two Alluring Flower Moths, photographing one with my camera. Several trees -- oaks as well as Longleaf Pines -- were downed from Hurricane Milton. 

These are my cell-phone photographs (216 of them in 183 records), which are GPS-enabled.

Note: I photographed dozens of Coastal Plain Honeycombhead plants; each record here is believed to represent a different individual.

*Quercus macrocarpa* ("Large-fruited Oak"), Bur Oak

Bur Oak is by far the most widespread of any oak species in North America, ranging from as far north as New Brunswick, Canada to as far south as southern Texas. This tree is often identified by the ways their leaves are shaped, often having large sinuses in the centermost part of the leaf, but shape can be variable. It can heavily resemble *Quercus bicolor*, Swamp White Oak and *Quercus alba*, American White Oak, but Swamp Whites lack the deep lobing of Burs and American White Oaks can be distinguished by the lobes on their leaves, which are often shaped like fingers.
It can also resemble *Quercus muehlenbergii*, Chinkapin Oak when young, but Chinkapin Oaks have ever occurred naturally once in Minnesota and haven't been seen since aside from urban and boulevard plantations.
I found this one growing alongside some *Fraxinus*, Ash, *Quercus ellipsoidalis* Hill's/Northern Pin Oak, *Quercus rubra*, Northern Red Oak, and *Acer rubrum*, Red Maple.

description:
*Quercus bicolor* ("Two-colored Oak"), Swamp White Oak

This species is somewhat commonly found in southern Minnesota, but has been introduced to the northern part of the state. It's currently labeled as a "State Special Concern" species, due to wild populations being at risk. How to identify this tree with the bark, which appears loose and papery when young, but it becomes grayer and more coarse with age. Leaves have uniform lobes, distinguishing it from *Quercus macrocarpa*, Bur Oak since they lack any deep lobes. The undersides of the leaf have dense white hairs that are soft to the touch, hence the scientific name: *Quercus bicolor*, which is a reference to the undersides of the leaves.
The acorns also grow from a long stalk, further distinguishing them from Bur Oaks, which lack the long stalks.
They tolerate moist climates, hence their common name and are commonly planted as urban or boulevard trees and are also used in forest restoration to help against threats like EAB.

description:
The Coast Live Oaks on the Monterey Peninsula are having a bumper crop of acorns this year. It should be a good winter for the Acorn Woodpeckers and other animals that depend on acorns. 

My favorite Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) observations:

Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) A.k.a. CLO, is a native, long-lived tree (up to 125 - 250 years) in the High-latitude Oaks (Subgenus Quercus) and Beech (Fagaceae) family. Quercus agrifolia is by far the most common Oak tree on the Monterey Peninsula, CA. Leaves are evergreen, oval, cupped or spoon-shaped (adaxially convex). “Hairy armpits” at leaf veins on underside of CLO leaf distinguishes it from other Quercus species. Margins of mature leaves have sharp spines that are very noticeable when you sit in the leaf litter. Acorns (fruits) are long and slender.

Per Jepson eFlora: Coast Live Oak grows "(6)10--25 m, evergreen; top wide; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2.5--6(9) cm; petiole 4--15 mm; blade generally widely elliptic to round, generally adaxially convex, +- dull green, abaxially glabrous to densely tomentose, dull, pale green, tip rounded to spine-toothed, margin rolled under or not, weakly spine-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--16 mm wide, 8--15 mm deep, obconic, scales thin, +- not tubercled, +- glabrous, +- brown; nut 25--35 mm, slender, ovoid, distally acute, shell woolly inside; mature in year 1. "

Jepson eFlora https://ucjeps.berkeley.edu/eflora/eflora_display.php?tid=40530

Many organisms call CLO home. There is a whole INat project called "The wonderful diversity of life on Coast Live Oak" https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/the-wonderful-diversity-of-life-on-coast-live-oak. For example,

What causes those fuzzy, white "hairy armpits" where primary vein meets 2ndary veins? Answer: Mite Apartments. Per INat fredwatson: "the prevailing hypothesis is that they function as dolmatia - places for arthopods to live - in this case, mites. There's an idea that the mites either eat fungi or prey on herbivores that would otherwise damage the leaf. A 2020 paper by Coltharp et al. found support for the dolmatium hypothesis, but didn't find support for the predation or fungivory - perhaps because of small sample size and not necessarily because the process doesn't occur. So, mites live there, and there might be a benefit to the tree."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

description:
With Don Fraser; a visit to see what was around. This was our final stop, after spending all our previous time in the hydric flatwoods along Retriever Road. We wanted sandhills, so we visited the area around the Gopher Road kestrel nest box, where we spent a little more than an hour (with not much happening). Still hoping for a Withlacoochee Grasshopper, I focused on finding grasshoppers (finding more toothpick grasshoppers than I had ever seen previously in one day), but I think I again struck out on _withlacoocheensis_. (I have decided to defocus on this species and sooner or later, I may luck upon one). I found an Eastern Fence Lizard, which is always a nice find. I resisted photographing every yellow flower as I searched for Alluring Schinia Moths, but I did photograph several as I need to learn the different species (and thanks as always, @jayhorn). We left at 1351, when the weather was sunny and 84 degrees ("feels like" 86), with a light breeze.

These are my cell-phone images, which are GPS-enabled. In some cases, I am uploading a cell-phone image just to have the precise location, and I will later upload my (superior) camera images.

description:
I find the shape of Oak leaves endlessly fascinating, as have many artists over the centuries. This one, from a White Oak I believe, is particularly lovely. I could make a huge collection of photographs of leaves like this on the ground at this time of year - no two alike. 

My observations of Oak leaves, especially White Oaks, don't attract much attention from those that identify trees (in fact none of my White Oak postings has gotten even a single ID from anyone), but I just can't help submitting fine examples now and again. They are so evocative of being in these woods, and it cheers me up to see them again when I can't get back out amongst them in person sometimes. 

This beautiful leaf was on a lonely footpath just above the floodplain near the downstream end of Cross Creek County Park, Washington County, in the rolling hills of the Allegheny Plateau, elevation about 299 meters (981 feet). These woods are a mixed mesophytic deciduous second growth forest with various Maple and Oak species, along with Beech, Hickory, Walnut, and Elm (at least as I have identified so far). The oaks in this location make quite a spectacular show of colour at this time of year, in late October.

Interior Live Oak (Quercus wislizeni), a.k.a Chapparal Oak, is a native Oak in the High-latitude Oaks (Quercus) Subgenus and in the Red Oaks (Lobatae) Section. It is found in Foothill Woodland and Chaparral plant communities. Leaves are mostly pliant and flat (not stiff and concave like Coast Live Oak, Quercus agrifolia), evergreen with smooth or spiny margins, dark green above and lighter below, and 1-4 inches long. Mature acorn is slender, about 1.25 inches long, cup covers almost half the nut, and acorn matures in second year. Acorn diagram: http://floranorthamerica.org/File:FNA03_P83_Quercus_pg_453.jpeg.

Indigenous people had many uses for this plant, medicinally and as food. 23 traditional uses are described here: http://naeb.brit.org/uses/search/?string=Quercus+wislizeni

Per Jepson eFlora: "Habit: Shrub 2--4(6) m or tree generally 10--22 m, evergreen; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2--5 cm; petiole 3--15 mm; blade generally oblong to elliptic or lanceolate, adaxially glabrous, shiny, generally dark green, abaxially glabrous, +- shiny, yellow-green, tip generally acute, abruptly pointed, margin entire to spine-toothed, rarely wavy. Fruit: cup 12--18 mm wide, 12--16 mm deep, cup-shaped to hemispheric, scales not tubercled, +- thin; nut 20--40 mm, cylindric-ovoid, ovoid, or +- obconic, distally acute to +- obtuse, shell woolly inside; mature in year 2."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

description:
Thought I would start adding notes to some of these now to help with ID tips and overall info of the species, especially for helping beginners on here. If you see any wrong info or think there's important details that need to be added, feel free to let me know!

*Quercus ellipsoidalis* ("Elliptic Oak"), Hill's/Northern Pin Oak. 

A common species found throughout central and southern Minnesota, but also found in the northern part of the state as well. This species can be identified with their leaves which have mostly C-shaped sinuses, distinguishing it from *Quercus rubra*, the Northern Red Oak. Their acorns are small and ovoid to globose in shape. They can also be found to have rings on the end opposite of the acorn cap, but are variable, having mostly none, but can be found to have 1 ring commonly and can sometimes be found to have 2 rings. Maybe 3 to 4 rings rarely, but I've yet to come across this. I'll update this when I study more of these acorns. All gathered acorns pictured here are about half an inch in length. The caps also cover about half the acorn, distinguishing it from species like Northern Red Oak. They are mostly found in drier upland areas (a good way to remember this is the name "Hill's Oak", which implies it grows on hills where they're found naturally).

A similar, almost identical species, *Quercus coccinea*, the Scarlet Oak, occurs in nearby states as far west as the very eastern part of Wisconsin, but never in Minnesota naturally, but can be found as boulevard or urban planted trees. Their acorns are said to be bigger, getting up to an inch long commonly and having 3 - 4 rings much more commonly than not.
*Quercus palustris*, Southern Pin/Swamp Spanish Oak, another similar species, can be found in Minnesota as boulevard or urban planted trees. Hill's Oak acorns can be longer and narrower than Southern Pin Oaks. Leaves are also extremely similar, almost identical, but the lobes are sometimes are narrower and sinuses can also be U-shaped as well. They also tolerate swampy areas better than Hill's Oaks.

This particular one was found with patches of Highbush Blackberries (Sect. Arguti) nearby, likely *Rubus recurvans*, Recurved Blackberry but could also be *Rubus frondosus*, Fronded/Yankee Blackberry, but that is yet to be determined. Will be updated once the species is determined. Also found *Pinus banksiana*, Jack Pine growing alongside these Hill's Oaks (will add observation in the spring when it gets warmer).

Muller's Oak (Quercus cornelius-mulleri) A.k.a. Desert Scrub Oak. Formerly called Quercus dumosa.
It is a native oak in White Oaks (Section Quercus) and in the Beech (Fagaceae) family that grows up to 3 meters (10 feet) tall, generally in granitic soils, in chaparral and pinyon woodland plant communities. It is a bushy, shrubby, and densely branched with tangled twigs. Leaves are evergreen, leathery and thick, oblong, ovate, or narrowly obovate with margins entire or 4--6-toothed. Leaves are adaxially (upper surface) sparsely puberulent and abaxially (underside) whitish and densely fine-tomentose. Habitat is chaparral and pinyon woodland, generally growing in granitic soils. Muller's oak was segregated from the Quercus dumosa complex in 1981 and was found to warrant species status of its own.

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

"The 25,500-acre Pioneertown Mountains Preserve descends from the high piney 7,800-foot ridges into the Pioneertown Valley. The small community of Pioneertown is surrounded by conservancy-owned volcanic mesas, the Sawtooth Mountains, and preserve lands leading to the San Bernardino National Forest. The preserve has year-round riparian corridors in Pipes Canyon and Little Morongo Canyon. It is an important landscape linkage between Joshua Tree National Park, San Bernardino National Forest, and the Big Horn Mountains Bureau of Land Management Wilderness.
In 2006, the vast majority of the Joshua trees, pinyon pines and junipers at Pioneertown Mountains Preserve were killed in a 70,000-acre lightning-caused fire of unprecedented magnitude. Today, much of the preserve is going through natural vegetation succession. Some scientists predict that fire succession and climate change will favor scrub oak and Joshua tree plant communities that may replace the pinyon forests. The fire laid bare the region’s rich geological backbone."

Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) A.k.a. CLO, is a native, long-lived tree (up to 125 - 250 years) in the High-latitude Oaks (Subgenus Quercus) and Beech (Fagaceae) family. Quercus agrifolia is by far the most common Oak tree on the Monterey Peninsula, CA. Leaves are evergreen, oval, cupped or spoon-shaped (adaxially convex). “Hairy armpits” at leaf veins on underside of CLO leaf distinguishes it from other Quercus species. Margins of mature leaves have sharp spines that are very noticeable when you sit in the leaf litter. Acorns (fruits) are long and slender.

Per Jepson eFlora: Coast Live Oak grows "(6)10--25 m, evergreen; top wide; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2.5--6(9) cm; petiole 4--15 mm; blade generally widely elliptic to round, generally adaxially convex, +- dull green, abaxially glabrous to densely tomentose, dull, pale green, tip rounded to spine-toothed, margin rolled under or not, weakly spine-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--16 mm wide, 8--15 mm deep, obconic, scales thin, +- not tubercled, +- glabrous, +- brown; nut 25--35 mm, slender, ovoid, distally acute, shell woolly inside; mature in year 1. "

Many organisms call CLO home. There is a whole INat project called "The wonderful diversity of life on Coast Live Oak" https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/the-wonderful-diversity-of-life-on-coast-live-oak. For example,

What causes those fuzzy, white "hairy armpits" where primary vein meets 2ndary veins? Answer: Mite Apartments. Per INat fredwatson: "the prevailing hypothesis is that they function as dolmatia - places for arthopods to live - in this case, mites. There's an idea that the mites either eat fungi or prey on herbivores that would otherwise damage the leaf. A 2020 paper by Coltharp et al. found support for the dolmatium hypothesis, but didn't find support for the predation or fungivory - perhaps because of small sample size and not necessarily because the process doesn't occur. So, mites live there, and there might be a benefit to the tree."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

Coast Live Oak (Quercus agrifolia) A.k.a. CLO, is a native, long-lived tree (up to 125 - 250 years) in the High-latitude Oaks (Subgenus Quercus) and Beech (Fagaceae) family. Quercus agrifolia is by far the most common Oak tree on the Monterey Peninsula, CA. Leaves are evergreen, oval, cupped or spoon-shaped (adaxially convex). “Hairy armpits” at leaf veins on underside of CLO leaf distinguishes it from other Quercus species. Margins of mature leaves have sharp spines that are very noticeable when you sit in the leaf litter. Acorns (fruits) are long and slender.

Per Jepson eFlora: Coast Live Oak grows "(6)10--25 m, evergreen; top wide; trunk bark furrowed, +- checkered, +- gray. Leaf: 2.5--6(9) cm; petiole 4--15 mm; blade generally widely elliptic to round, generally adaxially convex, +- dull green, abaxially glabrous to densely tomentose, dull, pale green, tip rounded to spine-toothed, margin rolled under or not, weakly spine-toothed. Fruit: cup 10--16 mm wide, 8--15 mm deep, obconic, scales thin, +- not tubercled, +- glabrous, +- brown; nut 25--35 mm, slender, ovoid, distally acute, shell woolly inside; mature in year 1. "

Many organisms call CLO home. There is a whole INat project called "The wonderful diversity of life on Coast Live Oak" https://www.inaturalist.org/projects/the-wonderful-diversity-of-life-on-coast-live-oak. For example,

What causes those fuzzy, white "hairy armpits" where primary vein meets 2ndary veins? Answer: Mite Apartments. Per INat fredwatson: "the prevailing hypothesis is that they function as dolmatia - places for arthopods to live - in this case, mites. There's an idea that the mites either eat fungi or prey on herbivores that would otherwise damage the leaf. A 2020 paper by Coltharp et al. found support for the dolmatium hypothesis, but didn't find support for the predation or fungivory - perhaps because of small sample size and not necessarily because the process doesn't occur. So, mites live there, and there might be a benefit to the tree."

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.

There are two observations of Quercus cedrosensis in Sycuan Peak Ecological Reserve, which I thought was interesting because the nearest population is near Otay Mountain, about 12mi/20km away.

I think that this is an Engelmann oak or hybrid that looks off because it's growing on a southwest-facing slope on mostly-granitic, rocky soil.
I tend to call oaks like these Q. x acutidens. But I don't know that I fully understand how to distinguish them from Q. berberidifolia.
I think this is Q. engelmannii and probably looks a little strange because it's growing on a southwest facing slope.

Muller's Oak (Quercus cornelius-mulleri) A.k.a. Desert Scrub Oak. Formerly called Quercus dumosa.
It is a native oak in White Oaks (Section Quercus) and in the Beech (Fagaceae) family that grows up to 3 meters (10 feet) tall, generally in granitic soils, in chaparral and pinyon woodland plant communities. It is a bushy, shrubby, and densely branched with tangled twigs. Leaves are evergreen, leathery and thick, oblong, ovate, or narrowly obovate with margins entire or 4--6-toothed. Leaves are adaxially (upper surface) sparsely puberulent and abaxially (underside) whitish and densely fine-tomentose. Habitat is chaparral and pinyon woodland, generally growing in granitic soils. Muller's oak was segregated from the Quercus dumosa complex in 1981 and was found to warrant species status of its own.

OAKs (genus Quercus) in general, have a worldwide distribution in Mediterranean climates.

Quercus (Oak) are in the Beech (Fagaceae) family.
Those found in Monterey County are in three groups: Red (or Black) Oaks, Intermediate Oaks, and White Oaks. Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks have acorns that generally mature over a 2 year period (Coast Live Oak is an exception to this rule). White Oaks have acorns that mature in a single season. Most Red Oaks and Intermediate Oaks are evergreen (California Black Oak being the exception). White Oaks may be either evergreen or deciduous. Hybrid forms are common. All oaks are monoecious, with conspicuous male flowers. Female flowers are found in the axils of the leaves near the tips of the new stems.
